text: The antagonists here are doctors who will not wash their hands. That is the film's real conflict, and it is a strange engine for a 1936 studio drama: a chemist without a medical degree telling physicians that invisible things are killing their patients, and physicians treating the suggestion as an insult. Disease is the subject; professional pride is the drama. With eighty-six minutes and a laboratory, the picture has almost no incident to offer, so it puts everything on speech and on the face of a man being right too early - which is where its recognition went, to the lead performance and to the story. What survives is less the science than the shape of the resistance: the long stretch during which evidence exists, is presented, and is refused by people with every reason to want it true.

A boy who has finished high school and begun nothing decides, in the meantime, to be Italian. He sings opera at the dinner table, races bicycles, and exhausts everyone who loves him. The affectation is the film's argument rather than its gag: four friends holding diplomas and no plans, filling a summer with a borrowed identity because the local one on offer looks like a sentence already passed. Peter Yates keeps the comedy quick and lets the ache sit underneath it, mostly in the father, who cannot find a single word for a son quoting a language he does not speak. The screenplay prizes came, and the National Society of Film Critics called it the year's best film - unusual company for something this unhurried. A hundred and one minutes in which nobody's future arrives.

A young carabiniere is handed paperwork: deliver two children from Milan to an orphanage in Sicily. That is the whole assignment, and the film runs the length of the country. Gianni Amelio lets the transfer turn into an accidental custody - three people in transit, one of them responsible, none of them consulted - while refusing every consolation the setup invites. The girl is eleven, and what was done to her stays outside the frame; what the film shows instead is the cost, to a stranger, of being gentle on a schedule. Italy arrives as motorway restaurants, waiting rooms, borrowed hours. It took the Grand Prix at Cannes and the Italian awards for film and direction, though the reason to sit with it is smaller than that: a man who was only supposed to sign a form, discovering he is the only adult in the car.

In a Manhattan teaching hospital, doctors keep turning up dead, and the institution is too busy to register it. The man who might have noticed is the chief of medicine, who has already decided he does not want to live. The film plays this as comedy and means it - the deaths register as one more administrative failure in a place where failure is the weather, and the mystery mostly exists to keep the corridors moving. What holds it together is the talk: long, furious, articulate speech from a man with nothing left to protect. The prizes it carries are for that writing and that lead performance, plus a Silver Bear, and it later entered the National Film Registry. Into the middle of it walks Barbara, whose father lies comatose upstairs, and toward whom the chief finds himself drawn against every conclusion he has reached.

A wedding arrives, and it is not the happy ending - it is the loss, and the person it happens to is not the bride. Claudia Weill builds eighty-eight minutes around a departure most films treat as a subplot: one roommate marries and moves out, and the other is left with the apartment, the rent, and photography jobs too small to become the career she wanted. The scale is deliberate. Nothing escalates. The crisis is that a friendship has quietly been demoted, and both women can feel it happening while neither will say so. It took an audience award in Toronto and a place on the National Film Registry. The comedy lives in small humiliations, and the weight in the negotiations of a woman learning what her days look like when nobody else is in the apartment to shape them.

Two people are in love with the same man, both of them know it, and neither intends to make him choose. The arrangement is the film: a doctor in middle age and a recently divorced woman with a career, each holding a portion of a young artist's week, each deciding the portion is worth the arithmetic. Made in Britain in 1971, it is far more interested in that arithmetic than in scandal. The register is domestic, adult and faintly tired, and the costs are counted in ordinary units - a weekend, a telephone that has to be answered, an evening where somebody is being brave about something. Its direction and its two leads were honored, and it sits on the BFI's hundred British films. What stays afterwards is how reasonably everybody behaves, and how little that helps.

Two and a half hours are given to a murder investigation with almost no interest in solving anything. The crime is unbearable - a child, in a quiet French town - and Bruno Dumont places it early, then turns the camera on everything surrounding it: fields, weather, meals, the slow face of a detective who seems to absorb the case rather than pursue it. Mystery supplies the frame; what fills it is closer to endurance, and the length is method rather than indulgence. Cannes gave it the Grand Prix and both acting prizes, and a European award went to its cinematography. That patience is the film's entire proposition, and it is not a neutral one. It looks at ordinary bodies and ordinary daylight for longer than is comfortable, and it does not blink.

Montreal, and a kid from a working-class Jewish family who has decided that owning land is the same thing as being somebody. The film follows the arithmetic of that belief without softening it: Duddy hustles, charms, borrows and uses, and the people fond of him are spent along the way. It is a comedy, which is the hard part - the laughs come out of his energy, and the energy is precisely what does the damage. Ted Kotcheff keeps antisemitism in the frame as the pressure that produced the hunger rather than as an alibi for it, and lets the family scenes run long enough that the trade being made becomes visible. It took the Golden Bear, and the writing awards followed. Two hours in the company of somebody whose charm is a bill that other people keep paying.

Dementia arrives in this house as one more item on a list that was already too long. The woman holding the list is May Sun, in her forties, running a household in Hong Kong, and her father-in-law's Alzheimer's becomes hers to manage alongside everything else nobody else volunteered for. Ann Hui refuses both of the available modes, the tragedy and the lesson, and stays with the adjustments: what gets rearranged this week, what is quietly given up. Illness here is not a scene but a schedule. The film swept the year's best-film prizes at home and at the Golden Horse, and its lead took a Silver Bear. Its original title, 女人，四十, names a woman and an age and nothing else, which turns out to be the exact size of what it is looking at.

The car is the whole architecture: one of them drives, one of them sits behind, and every conversation they have happens without eye contact. Hired man in front, employer in back - that geometry is what the film is about, and it lets affection and hierarchy occupy the same enclosed space until they have finished ruining each other. Adapted from L. P. Hartley, it treats English class as a physical fact rather than a theme: who opens the door, who is addressed by surname, who is permitted to look tired. A socialite alone inside a large life begins to need the man paid to move her around it, and need is the one currency the arrangement cannot price. It took the Palme d'Or. The interest now is in watching two people mismanage a closeness that neither of them is allowed to name.

Sheffield, after the steel: men with nothing left to sell but the bodies that used to do the selling for them. The plan is one night, one strip show, cash in hand, and the film understands it as a joke and a humiliation at once, without letting go of either. The comedy is structural rather than decorative - every laugh returns to the same question of what a man is worth once the thing he was paid for has shut down, which is why the preparation is funnier than the performance could be. Ninety-one minutes, and the best material is in the waiting. It took best film at the European Film Awards and a place on the BFI's hundred British films, and the fame that followed has flattened it into a single image of men standing in a line. The film underneath is smaller, colder and better than the image.

Everything at stake is a gesture: whether a private grief must be performed in public, and who has standing to decide. Diana is dead, the country wants mourning it can see, and the film stays indoors with the two people negotiating the gap - a monarch and a new prime minister, a generation apart, neither of them in control of the week. Stephen Frears keeps the register dry and lets the comedy come from protocol: drafts, telephone calls, advisers, the choreography of who may ring whom. What lifts it above reconstruction is that the older woman's position gets its fullest hearing rather than being staged as an obstacle, so that restraint arrives as a claim about respect and not merely as coldness. The lead performance took the Academy Award and a Volpi Cup, and it is built almost entirely on withholding.

A film released in 1933 that ends in 1933, having opened in the final hours of the nineteenth century. That span is its real subject - not the Boer War or the Titanic or Victoria's funeral as events, but the sensation of one London household being carried through them and totting up the bill. The device is the turning year: a drawing room, a newspaper, a son suddenly grown. It produces a chronicle rather than a plot, and its first audiences had personally lived through most of what it covers, an intimacy no revival can restore. The Academy gave it picture and directing awards while Hollywood was still deciding what a prestige film should sound like. Watched now, the machinery is plainly visible, and what still works is the calendar itself, and the speed at which a lifetime is made to pass.

A playwright agrees to carry money into Nazi Germany because a friend asked her to. That is the whole operation, and Fred Zinnemann films it as one: a train, a package, a border, several hours of a woman with none of a spy's equipment trying to look like a tourist. The suspense is procedural and almost entirely interior. Around the errand sits the friendship it came from - two women who met young, one of whom went to Europe and turned into something the other can only partly follow - assembled out of the loops and gaps of recollection rather than in sequence. The lead performance, the photography and the costumes were all honored, and the writing took its prizes too. The politics stay stubbornly personal, sized to what one person can carry across one frontier in a piece of luggage.
